Neonates of the Roughskin skate emerge from their egg cases at a total length of 25 centimeters [Lb = 25 centimeters], a size that reflects the substantial yolk investment during the prolonged internal incubation period. Available data indicate that this length at birth is consistent with the relatively large egg cases characteristic of the genus Dipturus, which provide the developing embryo with ample nutrient reserves. Following emergence, the young individuals immediately commence independent foraging, feeding on small benthic invertebrates. Field surveys suggest that the initial growth phase is rapid, with juveniles doubling in length within the first few years after the yolk-sac resorption is complete. The size at which the yolk-dependent embryo transitions to exogenous feeding appears to be tightly linked to the total length at birth, as the nutritional reserves must sustain the embryo through organogenesis and blastula-stage development. At a controlled water temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C], the age at birth, which encompasses the entire period from egg fertilisation to the onset of exotrophic transition, has been estimated at 590 days [ab = 590 days], a remarkably extended incubation period that underscores the slow developmental rate typical of many deepwater elasmobranchs.

As females progress through their life cycle, the ultimate total length they attain is a critical life-history parameter, with the largest documented individuals reaching 264 centimeters [Li = 264 centimeters]. This impressive size distinguishes the Roughskin skate as one of the most substantial members of its genus, and it is comparable to the maximum dimensions reported for other large-bodied rajiforms inhabiting continental slope environments. The attainment of this asymptotic length is a gradual process, with growth rates decelerating markedly after the onset of gonadal maturation. Examination of museum specimen series indicates that females continue to increase in girth and overall body mass well after reaching reproductive maturity, though linear extension slows considerably. The estimated maximum lifespan under natural conditions, measured at a stable temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C], is approximately 27 years [am = approximately 27 years], a value that aligns well with the expectations of a K-selected species exhibiting delayed maturation, low natural mortality, and relatively low fecundity. This longevity is consistent with the slow metabolic pace inferred from the species' cold-water habitat.

Sexual maturation in this species is marked by distinct size thresholds that differ between the sexes, reflecting the energetic demands of reproductive activity. For females, the total length at puberty is recorded at 215 centimeters [Lp = 215 centimeters], a value that represents a substantial proportion of the ultimate length attained by adult females. This delayed maturation, requiring roughly three-quarters of the potential lifespan before the onset of ovarian maturation, is a pattern commonly observed in large, slow-growing elasmobranchs where reproductive activation is postponed until a sufficiently large body size is achieved to accommodate gestation. Males, by contrast, reach puberty at a smaller dimension, with the total length at puberty being 195 centimeters [Lp = 195 centimeters]. This sexual dimorphism in maturation size is typical of many skate species and likely reflects the different energetic commitments associated with male versus female reproductive roles. The onset of testicular recrudescence in males occurs at a body length that still allows considerable further somatic growth before the individual approaches its asymptotic size.

Reproductive output in the Roughskin skate is relatively modest compared to many teleost fishes, a characteristic that underscores its vulnerability to overexploitation. Under a controlled thermal regime of 6 °C [T = 6 °C], the maximum reproductive rate has been reported as approximately 50 pups per year [Ri = approximately 50 pups per year], a value that appears to be influenced by maternal body size and nutritional condition. This annual fecundity is delivered through the repeated deposition of fertilised egg cases, with individual females producing multiple clutches over the course of a single breeding season. The egg cases are typically deposited on soft substrates on the continental shelf and slope, where they undergo the prolonged incubation period of 590 days [ab = 590 days] at 6 °C [T = 6 °C] that was noted earlier. Given this extended incubation, the total number of offspring that successfully hatch from a single year's reproductive effort is substantially lower than the raw fecundity estimate might suggest, as egg case mortality from predation and physical disturbance can be considerable.

Comparative analyses with other members of the Rajidae family highlight the unusual life-history strategy of the Roughskin skate. The attainment of an ultimate total length of 264 centimeters [Li = 264 centimeters] places it near the upper end of the size spectrum for the genus Dipturus, a status that carries implications for its trophic role as a benthic predator on continental slopes. The substantial size at emergence of 25 centimeters [Lb = 25 centimeters] confers a survival advantage by reducing vulnerability to gape-limited predators during the earliest life stages, a trait that is proportionally large relative to the adult size. The sexual maturation sizes, with females attaining puberty at 215 centimeters [Lp = 215 centimeters] and males at 195 centimeters [Lp = 195 centimeters], represent approximately 81 percent and 74 percent of the female ultimate length, respectively, indicating that both sexes delay reproduction until a significant portion of somatic growth is complete. This suite of life-history traits - large body size, slow growth, late maturation, low fecundity, and extended longevity - positions the Roughskin skate as a quintessential K-selected species, highly sensitive to any increase in adult or juvenile mortality.
